arguments.name: Habermas avoids Christian/non-Christian labels
arguments.conclusion: Habermas does not classify scholars as Christians versus non-Christians but rather as liberal versus conservative on the resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: He has no right to judge who is a Christian, since God separates wheat from tares.
He uses categories like left/right, conservative/liberal, and scholarly spectrum instead.
Scholars who affirm the resurrection are placed on the right and those who deny it on the left, regardless of self-identification.

st1.quote: So I will never point to you or somebody else and say, "Hey Dale, I got a problem. I hear you're not a Christian."

st2.quote: I might say left and right. I might say conservative liberal. I might say across the scholarly spectrum.

st3.quote: The old statement that says um when we get to heaven, we're going to find a lot more people that we knew for sure were going to hell or we were wrong and they're up there in heaven.

st4.quote: So anybody who thinks I'm saying that they're questioning before they ask me my view of what I meant.

st5.quote: But you don't do it for the other side. We got too much of that.

st6.quote: I'm not reading your mind. I'm not judging you. I don't think that's that should ever be done.

st7.quote: if you find that anywhere in one of my books, tell me and we'll put it in the list of ARTA to be changed

st8.quote: I might get nailed from the right [clears throat] by not being conservative enough on my view of this or that. And then I get viewed from the left by saying I have a statement that, you know, I'm at this school named Liberty University.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Risen Jesus and Future Hope / minimal-facts method, 2003

or1.quote: I can't say Christians and non-Christians.
or1.why: A methodological self-description about labeling, not a restatement of his resurrection argument.

or2.quote: When I did this originally, I listed the liberals first and the conservatives second.
or2.why: Adds autobiographical detail about his citation practice, not new evidence for the resurrection.

arguments.weakest_link: The premise that his other interviews consistently avoid the framing rests on the host's anecdotal review rather than a systematic check.
arguments.develop_next: Provide a documented count of every occurrence of 'Christian/non-Christian' across his published corpus to show the single podcast instance is anomalous.

arguments.name: Habermas cites critics more often than believers
arguments.conclusion: Volume three cites critical scholars more frequently than believing scholars, though not because there are more critical names.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: He counted the citations and found more from critical than believing commentators.
He originally listed liberals first and conservatives second in his source list.
The claim is about frequency of citation, not headcount of scholars.

st1.quote: I have more citations from critical people than I do from believing commentators.

st2.quote: What I mean is I might cite man 60 times and the leading evangelical 22.

st3.quote: I went back and counted volume three. I went all the way through it.

st4.quote: I use I have more citations from critical people than I do from believing commentators.

st5.quote: Yeah, but that's not what I meant. I meant more citations >> exactly >> by critics and citations >> by believers.

st6.quote: So what I mean is not I have more liberal people than than Evangels. I mean, I cite them more often.

st7.quote: I wrote that down and I have it on a sheet of paper where I counted com counted.

st8.quote: Ben can verify it because he had the originals.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (citation methodology), 1996

or1.quote: I went back and counted volume three.
or1.why: A specific citation-count claim about his own volume, not a restatement of prior argument.

or2.quote: I might cite man 60 times and the leading evangelical 22.
or2.why: Brings a citation-frequency datum prior work does not use.

or4.quote: You said it was a ratio of 3 to one set.
or4.why: A ratio is offered informally but not formalized.

arguments.weakest_link: The count is self-reported and the exact number is disclaimed ('I don't know that number'), so the frequency claim is unverifiable as stated.
arguments.develop_next: Publish the actual citation tally with page-level references so the frequency claim can be independently checked.

arguments.name: Charity toward apparent misspeaking
arguments.conclusion: Critics should apply the principle of charity to a single apparent misspeaking rather than treating it as revealing Habermas's real view.
arguments.speaker: Dale (host) and Gary Habermas
premises: Habermas's other interviews consistently avoid the Christian/non-Christian framing.
A charitable reader would examine the full context.
Critics demand multiple clear instances but rely on one cloudy one.

st1.quote: Well, I think the principle of charity, that's what I call for, right?

st2.quote: So, anyone who's being charitable would look at the full context.

st3.quote: in 3700 pages, you should be able to find five more like that.

st4.quote: Instead of using one cloudy one, why don't you give me five more clear ones?

st5.quote: But if people would just give me the grace to be talking like they would do for one of their own quote unquote kind.

st6.quote: I think it was just one one time you sort of misspoke on a on a podcast

st7.quote: if it can be taken either way in context, why don't you find five more places where I said it the the way you're blaming me with?

st8.quote: And you're the funny thing I all your other interviews you're you're clear. You never you never say that about the non-Christian versus Christian.

or1.quote: you've been perfectly consistent. There there's nothing in the book that says that.
or1.why: An interpretive-charity argument about a specific dispute, not a restatement of a prior argument.

or2.quote: I had to. Yeah, because I just wanted to get to the bottom of that when I was um finding out the truth and and you were vindicated, I found.
or2.why: Uses the host's review of the interview corpus as evidence.

arguments.weakest_link: The premise that the other interviews are consistently clear is asserted by the host, not demonstrated with citations.
arguments.develop_next: Give timestamps or transcripts from several other interviews showing the consistent framing, so the charity claim rests on data rather than assertion.

arguments.name: Notable scholarly quotes on bodily resurrection
arguments.conclusion: Several prominent scholars, including critics, affirm that Paul and the earliest Christians believed in a bodily resurrection.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: John Cook states Paul saw the same body described in the Gospels.
Dale Allison says Paul meant a bodily resurrection even though Allison is open to non-bodily views.
Tom Wright, Michael Licona, and Robert Gundry make similar strong bodily-resurrection comments.

st1.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st2.quote: my thesis is that Paul's view of the resurrection is that he saw the same body as described in the Gospels

st3.quote: Del Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the gospels do.

st4.quote: I think Paul meant bodily resurrection view.

st5.quote: You got to make this distinguish between what Paul said and somebody else going, "Well, Boltman says Paul believed bodily resurrection." No, he didn't.

st6.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.

st7.why: No kill condition or test is stated.

st8.quote: So does Mike Lakona. So does um uh Gundry and his book on S uh Robert Gundry.

arguments.prior_art: N.T. Wright, The Resurrection of the Son of God, 2003

or1.quote: The fact that Paul believes in bodily resurrection is very widely taught today.
or1.why: A variant of the Wright-style bodily-resurrection case, assembled by citation rather than argued anew.

or2.quote: Del Allison said Paul believed in bodily resurrection appearance like the gospels do.
or2.why: Uses Allison, Cook, Gundry and Licona as data points prior art does not collect together.

arguments.weakest_link: The premise that Allison and the others affirm bodily resurrection is supported by paraphrase rather than exact quoted text in context.
arguments.develop_next: Quote each scholar's sentence verbatim with page references so the convergence claim can be verified.

arguments.name: Presumption of innocence for historical sources
arguments.conclusion: Historical sources should generally be given the benefit of the doubt until shown otherwise, including skeptical sources.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: Outside religion, one normally listens before accusing a source of lying.
Habermas was himself a skeptic for about twenty years, including after his PhD, so he can think as a skeptic.
He has read more material against the resurrection than for it.

st1.quote: I would I would tend to the first view that at any and in any subject way outside of religion, I would tend to be inclined to listen and think

st2.quote: I was a skeptic for 10 straight years and a bit for 10 more after it off and on.

st3.quote: That was after I finished my PhD.

st4.quote: So, because I've come from that, I can think easier as a skeptic.

st5.quote: if I know something, especially in this subject, this this area to disagree, um, I'll say so.

st6.quote: But I think I tend toward the listening area, even with skeptics

st7.why: No test or kill condition is given.

st8.quote: I've read way more material by unbelievers than I have by believers.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus (burden-of-proof discussion), 1996

or1.quote: I think I tend toward the listening area, even with skeptics
or1.why: A variant of standard historiographical charity, applied to his own biography.

or2.quote: I got pretty close to that pretty close. So because I doubted for so long and so deeply that I could even come to that view.
or2.why: Brings autobiographical data (near-conversion to a Buddhist metaphysics) prior art does not use.

or3.quote: the late 70s and 80s argument that Buddhism provides the the specific metaphysical background for physics as science
or3.why: Touches a physics-Buddhism bridge, though only as biography.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from 'I was a skeptic and read critics' to 'sources should be presumed innocent' is a personal-disposition claim, not a normative argument.
arguments.develop_next: State the burden-of-proof rule explicitly and defend it against the standard historical-criticism objection that sources are tested, not presumed.

arguments.name: Early creedal tradition predates the Gospels
arguments.conclusion: The earliest Christian creeds about Jesus's death and resurrection predate the written Gospels and go back to the 30s AD.
arguments.speaker: Gary Habermas
premises: 1 Thessalonians, commonly dated before 50 AD, assumes its audience already knows the core Christological definitions.
Romans 10:9 and 1 Corinthians 15:3ff preserve early creedal material.
Even the Jesus Seminar holds that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed existed before Paul's conversion.

st1.quote: But I think to say the 30s before 40, very common.

st2.quote: because that's the most common date given to First Thessalonians.

st3.quote: They said that creed or its component parts was already in existence before Paul took his walk to Damascus.

st4.quote: So that presumes a previous material before first Corinth first Thessalonians.

st5.quote: But even the Jesus seminar says before he was converted.

st6.quote: I would think plus anywhere in the first 10 is pretty and I can give you a number of guys who will date it between 30.

st7.quote: if you say, "No, I like, you know, I like 33." Okay. Well, all you're going to do is make the gap smaller.

st8.quote: Well, Corinthians has come back for a lot of people to 53 AD. I mean, these earliest ones are pretty early.

arguments.prior_art: Gary Habermas, The Historical Jesus / 1 Corinthians 15 creedal argument, 1996

or1.quote: But I think to say the 30s before 40, very common.
or1.why: A variant of the standard early-creed argument, extended with dating details.

or2.quote: Even the Jesus Seminar holds that the 1 Corinthians 15 creed existed before Paul's conversion.
or2.why: Uses the Jesus Seminar's own vote as hostile-witness evidence prior art typically does not deploy.

arguments.weakest_link: The inference from the creed's pre-Pauline existence to the 30s date depends on the contested dating of 1 Thessalonians and on oral-transmission assumptions.
arguments.develop_next: Lay out the dating chain (crucifixion 30-33, creed before Paul's conversion, 1 Thessalonians before 50) with the specific scholarly sources for each link.
